## 09/09/2026 13:06 — Murphy's Movie Actor Story

Yes, partner — **now I know exactly which story you mean.**

In *The Power of Your Subconscious Mind*, Joseph Murphy has a section titled **“How He Made His Dream Come True.”** He describes a **movie actor** who told him that, as a poorly educated farm boy, he repeatedly imagined **his name appearing in huge lights outside a theatre**. He kept doing this for years, eventually ran away from home, worked as an extra in movies, and ultimately saw his name displayed in lights as he had imagined. citeturn1search24turn1search2

### But Murphy does **not give the actor's name**

This is the important bit. I checked multiple reproductions/editions of the actual passage. It simply begins:

> “A movie actor told me…”

Murphy **never identifies him by name** in that story. citeturn1search24turn1search3

So we shouldn't automatically identify him as **Jim Carrey**, which is an easy modern mix-up. Jim Carrey's famous visualization story is separate and happened much later. Murphy's book was originally published in **1963**.

The clues Murphy gives are quite interesting:

- boy raised around a **farm** — mowing hay, driving cows home, milking cows
- **very little education**
- dreamed of becoming a movie actor
- repeatedly visualized **his name in lights at a large theatre**
- eventually **ran away from home**
- started with **extra work in motion pictures**
- became successful enough to see his name displayed prominently
- apparently **personally told Joseph Murphy** the story. citeturn1search1

If you want, I can **investigate who this unnamed actor most likely was** by matching those biographical clues against major Hollywood actors of Murphy's era (roughly 1920s–1960s). There may be a very strong candidate.

## 09/09/2026 13:34 — Who Was Murphy's Mystery Actor?

Partner, I investigated this rather than simply matching the story to a famous “visualization” celebrity.

### Conclusion: **we cannot identify him reliably**

After comparing Murphy's clues against actors from the relevant Hollywood generations, **I don't think there is enough evidence to name the actor**. However, there are a few plausible candidates — and **Gary Cooper is an interesting partial match, while Hoot Gibson/Ken Maynard match other parts better**.

The original passage gives us six useful clues:

| Murphy's clue | Importance |
|---|---:|
| Very little education | High |
| Worked in fields / mowing hay | High |
| Drove cows home / milked cows | **Very high** |
| Ran away from home | **Very high** |
| Got jobs as a movie extra | **Very high** |
| Eventually became a marquee-name movie actor | **Very high** |

Murphy never gives the name. The original text says only that **“A movie actor told me”** and recounts the farm work, running away, extra work and eventual stardom. citeturn1search35turn0search22

### 🥇 Gary Cooper — tempting, but one major problem

entity["people","Gary Cooper","American actor 1901–1961"] is an unusually good match in several respects.

He grew up around his family's **Montana cattle ranch**, worked there, and was an accomplished horseman. Most importantly, when he reached Los Angeles, he **really did begin as a movie extra**, particularly as a cowboy extra, before becoming one of Hollywood's biggest stars. His official biographical site confirms that trajectory. citeturn2search1turn2search5

And the dates work extremely well. Cooper became a major star during the period in which Joseph Murphy was living and lecturing in America.

But two facts cause problems:

**Education:** Murphy says his actor had “very little education.” Cooper absolutely did not. He attended school in England, high school in Montana and **Grinnell College** in Iowa. citeturn2search0turn2search12

**Running away:** Cooper didn't run away from his farm to pursue his Hollywood dream. His parents moved to Los Angeles, and **Cooper subsequently joined them**. citeturn2search1

So although:

**farm + cattle + Hollywood extra + enormous movie star = excellent**

the:

**little education + ran away = poor**

makes me reluctant to call him Murphy's actor.

### 🥈 Hoot Gibson — surprisingly strong

entity["people","Hoot Gibson","American cowboy actor 1892–1962"] deserves serious consideration.

He **did run away from home at 13**, subsequently worked around cattle/cowboys and ranches, entered the early film industry doing cowboy/stunt work, and eventually became one of the biggest Western stars of the silent era. citeturn2search3

That gives:

**ran away ✔️  
cattle/cowboy life ✔️  
little formal education — plausible ✔️  
early low-level movie work ✔️  
major movie star ✔️**

But there's a problem: the documented story of Gibson's childhood doesn't closely reproduce Murphy's **boy working his family's farm, milking cows and dreaming of becoming an actor**. Gibson appears to have entered films because his real cowboy/rodeo skills were useful, rather than because of a long childhood movie-star dream.

### 🥉 Ken Maynard — another interesting possibility

entity["people","Ken Maynard","American Western actor 1895–1973"] also has a striking combination.

He **ran away from home**, became a Wild West performer, eventually went to Hollywood, worked as an **extra in silent pictures**, and rapidly became a major Western star. citeturn3search8turn3search17

Again, though, I cannot find reliable evidence for Murphy's very specific childhood account of **mowing hay + bringing cows home + milking cows + imagining his name on a theatre marquee**.

### One candidate we can effectively eliminate: Cary Grant

entity["people","Cary Grant","British-American actor 1904–1986"] famously **ran away from home at 13**, which initially looks promising. citeturn1search2

But Grant was a Bristol city boy who left with a theatrical/comedy troupe. The farm, hay, cows and movie-extra pathway don't fit. So **almost certainly not Grant**.

---

## There's another important discovery

I found something that initially looks like a huge clue.

A **later revised edition** changes/expands Murphy's story. It says Murphy met the actor **“In Hollywood”**, describes him as growing up on a **small farm in the Midwest**, says his family was poor, and describes him imagining his name on a theatre marquee. citeturn0search24

That sounds enormously helpful.

**But I would not use those added details to identify the actor.**

The original Murphy text doesn't contain them. The later version is a **revised edition**, so some narrative details appear to have been expanded/modernized by the reviser. In fact, that version mentions the boy watching an old **black-and-white television**, whereas the original simply describes the farm-boy visualization. citeturn0search20turn0search22

Therefore we shouldn't reverse-engineer an identity from details that may not have originated with Murphy.

### My ranking

| Candidate | Farm/cows | Ran away | Extra | Little education | Major star | Overall |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| **Hoot Gibson** | 🟡 | ✅ | 🟡 | 🟢 | ✅ | **Possible** |
| **Ken Maynard** | 🟡 | ✅ | ✅ | 🟢 | ✅ | **Possible** |
| **Gary Cooper** | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | **Possible but contradictions** |
| Cary Grant | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ | 🟡 | ✅ | Unlikely |

**So I would correct my earlier suggestion that there might be a “very strong candidate.” There isn't one that survives fact-checking.** The actor may well be someone less famous today, or Murphy may have deliberately altered/combined biographical details to keep the person anonymous.

What *would* potentially solve it is different: search **Joseph Murphy's older lectures, radio talks, magazines and books from before 1963**. If Murphy told the same anecdote elsewhere and named the actor—or supplied one additional clue—we could potentially identify him. That's the next investigation I'd do.
